course: CMU 21-254: Linear Algebra and Vector Calculus for Engineers
audience: SI leader teaching live on a whiteboard. This is not a student worksheet.
toneRule: Keep explanations very simple, verbal, and board-friendly. Avoid textbook phrasing unless the problem needs it.
title: Line Integrals, Conservative Fields, and Path Independence
sessionGoal: Students should be able to compute scalar and vector line integrals and use potential functions when a field is conservative.
quickStartIfUnprepared: Start with the difference: scalar line integral uses ds; vector line integral uses dr.
Do Problem 1 for scalar line integrals.
Do Problem 2 for direct vector line integral setup.
Do Problem 3 for conservative fields and path independence.
sayThisFirst: A scalar line integral adds up a scalar quantity along a curve.
A vector line integral measures how much a vector field pushes along the path.
For \(\int_C F\cdot dr\), plug in the curve and dot with \(r'(t)\).
If \(F=\nabla f\), then the line integral only depends on endpoints.
boardPlan: Write the two line-integral templates side by side.
Do one scalar line integral using \(ds=\|r'(t)\|dt\).
Do one vector line integral using \(F(r(t))\cdot r'(t)\).
Finish with a potential function and endpoint shortcut.
keyFormulas: Vector line integral: \(\int_C F\cdot dr=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r'(t)\,dt\).
For \(F=\langle P,Q\rangle\), conservative usually means \(P_y=Q_x\) on a nice region.
commonMistakes: Using \(ds\) in a vector line integral.
Forgetting to plug the curve into the field.
Using the endpoint shortcut before checking the field is conservative.
Subtracting endpoints in the wrong order.
notationWarnings: Use \(dr\) or \(F\cdot dr\) for vector line integrals.
For conservative fields, clearly name the potential function, often \(\phi\) or \(f\).

problems.title: Scalar line integral along a line segment
problems.studentPromptLatex: Let \(C\) be the line segment from \((0,0)\) to \((3,4)\). Compute \(\int_C (x+y)\,ds\).
problems.whatToSayBefore: Say: because this has \(ds\), we need the speed factor \(\|r'(t)\|\).

drawInstructions: Shade/mark that x+y is sampled along the segment.

commonMistakes: Using \(r'(t)\) as a vector instead of its length.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 8 for line integrals.

problems.title: Vector line integral by direct parametrization
problems.studentPromptLatex: Let \(F(x,y)=\langle y,x\rangle\) and let \(C\) be \(r(t)=(t,t^2)\), \(0\le t\le1\). Compute \(\int_C F\cdot dr\) directly.
problems.whatToSayBefore: Say: for \(F\cdot dr\), the recipe is field along the curve dotted with velocity.

drawInstructions: Draw the parabola y=x^2 from (0,0) to (1,1).
Put arrows on the curve from left to right.
Draw a few field arrows F=<y,x> near the curve.
Write F(r(t)) dot r'(t) beside the picture.

walkthrough.label: Plug the curve into the field
walkthrough.latex: Along the curve, \(x=t\) and \(y=t^2\), so \[F(r(t))=\langle t^2,t\rangle.\]

commonMistakes: Forgetting to plug \(x=t\), \(y=t^2\) into the field.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 8 for vector line integrals.

problems.title: Conservative field and endpoint shortcut
problems.studentPromptLatex: Let \(F(x,y)=\langle 2xy+3,x^2+4y\rangle\). Show that \(F\) is conservative, find a potential function \(\phi\), and compute \(\int_C F\cdot dr\) from \((0,1)\) to \((2,-1)\).
problems.whatToSayBefore: Say: if the field is conservative, the path itself does not matter. Only the start and end points matter.

drawInstructions: Draw two different paths from (0,1) to (2,-1).
Label both paths with the same endpoint value difference.

walkthrough.label: Check the conservative condition
walkthrough.latex: Here \(P=2xy+3\) and \(Q=x^2+4y\). \[P_y=2x,\qquad Q_x=2x.\] Since \(P_y=Q_x\), the field is conservative on \(\mathbb{R}^2\).

commonMistakes: Forgetting the \(g(y)\) term after integrating with respect to \(x\).
Using start minus end instead of end minus start.
Using the shortcut without first checking the field is conservative.

open.title: Adding things up along a path
say: An ordinary integral adds things up along the x-axis. A line integral adds things up along any curve.

There are two kinds, and the whole session hinges on telling them apart: ds adds up a quantity along the curve, like mass on a wire; F · dr adds up how much a field pushes you along the path, like work.

ask.q: You carry a box up a spiral staircase and back down to where you started. How much total work did gravity do?
ask.a: Zero. Gravity only cares about your change in height, and you ended where you started.

idea.title: ds measures the path; dr pushes along it
say: Both recipes start the same way: parametrize the curve and plug r(t) into whatever you're integrating.

With ds you multiply by the speed |r′(t)|, because you're adding up length-weighted values. With F · dr you dot with the velocity r′(t), because only the part of F along your direction of travel does work.
Some fields are gradients, like gravity. For those, the work only depends on where you start and end. That's the shortcut we'll earn at the end.
draw: Draw a curve with small arrows along it (the velocity) and a few field arrows F crossing it.
At one spot, split F into a piece along the curve and a piece across it. Label the 'along' piece 'does work'.
Write the two templates side by side: g · |r′| vs. F · r′.

ask.q: If F is perpendicular to the path everywhere, what is ∫ F · dr?
ask.a: 0: F never pushes along the path.

ask.q: Does reversing the direction of travel change ∫ g ds? ∫ F · dr?
ask.a: ∫ g ds stays the same; ∫ F · dr flips sign.

launch.say: Compute the ds line integral along the segment from (0, 0) to (3, 4).
circulate: Look for the missing factor of 5.
Check the parametrization runs from t = 0 to t = 1.

askFirst.a: ds, so we need the speed |r′(t)|.

ask.a: The segment has length 5, covered in 1 unit of t.
The value of x + y at the point we've reached at time t.
The midpoint (1.5, 2) has x + y = 3.5, the average value; times length 5 gives 17.5. ✓

steps.why: A ds integral is 'average value × length'. That makes a great check.

si19-p1.meaning: Think of a wire from (0, 0) to (3, 4) whose density is x + y. Its total mass is 35/2.

ifStuck.then: ask where the length of the segment shows up in their integral.

si19-p1.transition: Now the other kind: a field pushing along a curve.

launch.say: Compute ∫ F · dr along the parabola directly: field on the curve, dotted with velocity.
circulate: Check x = t and y = t² were substituted into F before dotting.

askFirst.a: No: F · dr uses the velocity vector r′(t) itself.

ask.q: Which way does the velocity point at t = 1?
ask.a: (1, 2): up and to the right, along the parabola.

steps.say: On the curve, F = ⟨y, x⟩ becomes ⟨t², t⟩.

ask.q: Why do we have to substitute?
ask.a: We only care about F at points on the curve.

ask.q: Is F helping or fighting the motion along the way?
Here's a surprise: F = ∇(xy). What's xy at the end minus the start?
ask.a: 1 · 1 − 0 · 0 = 1. The same answer, with no integral!

steps.why: That coincidence isn't one. It's exactly the shortcut the next problem is about.

si19-p2.meaning: Along the parabola the field always pushes forward, and the total push adds up to 1. Because F is a gradient, any path from (0, 0) to (1, 1) would give 1.

ifStuck.if: a student multiplies by the speed
ifStuck.then: compare with the template: F · dr uses r′(t), not |r′(t)|.

si19-p2.transition: Last one: recognize a gradient field on sight, find its potential, and skip the integral entirely.

launch.say: Show F is conservative, find a potential φ, and compute the integral from (0, 1) to (2, −1).
circulate: Check the + g(y) after integrating P in x.
End minus start, not start minus end.
Encourage checking ∇φ = F at the end.

askFirst.q: Which path does the problem give?
askFirst.a: None. That's a hint that the path doesn't matter.

steps.say: P = 2xy + 3, Q = x² + 4y. P_y = 2x = Q_x, so F is conservative on ℝ².

ask.a: Q_x − P_y is the 2D curl. Conservative fields have zero curl: no spinning.

steps.say: Integrate P in x: φ = x²y + 3x + g(y).

ask.a: Anything that depends only on y has x-derivative 0, so it could be hiding there.

steps.say: \(\phi_y=x^2+g'(y)\) must equal \(x^2+4y\), so \(g'(y)=4y\) and \(g=2y^2\). That gives \(\phi=x^2y+3x+2y^2\).
steps.why: The x² terms matching up is the conservative test succeeding in real time.

ask.q: What would the integral be around a closed loop?
ask.a: 0: the start and end are the same point.

si19-p3.meaning: F is the slope field of the landscape φ. Walking from (0, 1) to (2, −1) you climb from height 2 to height 4, whatever path you take, so the work is 2.

ifStuck.then: differentiate what they have in y and compare with Q term by term.

wrap.write: ds: multiply by |r′(t)| (mass, length, average). F · dr: dot with r′(t) (work, flow). Conservative (P_y = Q_x): integral = φ(end) − φ(start).

exit.a: For adding a scalar along a curve, like mass on a wire or arc length.

exit.q: When do we use F · dr?
exit.a: For work or flow of a vector field along a path.

exit.q: What changes when F is conservative?
exit.a: Only the endpoints matter; closed loops give 0.
